candidates.excerpt: When an AI agent gets stuck in a recursive loop or bungles a multi-step data pipeline, the failure is often blamed on the model. We assume it simply lacks the intelligence or the parameter count to complete the job. However, the root cause usually lies in the shape of the workflow and the rigid boundaries of the systems memory. Large language models generate confident, highly structured pros that aligns with human evaluation heristics. Because we instinctively equate linguistic fluency with logical accuracy, we often assume a plan is sound simply because it is well articulated. This creates a fluency trap where the quality of the pros masks a lack of underlying grounding. This diagram shows two distinct problem solving systems. On the left is internal reasoning, a static isolated process where the AI calculates an answer in a vacuum. On the right is external planning, a dynamic execution sequence where the system sequences operations against a shifting real world environment. A model can generate a logical internal monologue, but the only valid test of an agentic system is whether its architecture can execute that plan when the actual environment pushes back. For edge cases where a task has many viable paths or potential deadends, developers look to multiath architectures like state space search. This diagram shows a system testing multiple branches simultaneously to find the optimal route. It functions like a chess engine projecting multiple moves ahead to navigate high levels of state space complexity. However, maintaining these parallel traces multiplies API costs and adds significant orchestration complexity.
